appraisal_events.evidence: "ce ne fut pas ainsi qu'Elstir agit avec moi ; en vrai maître... il cherchait à extraire pour le meilleur enseignement des jeunes gens la part de vérité qu'elle contenait. Il préféra donc aux paroles qui auraient pu venger son amour-propre celles qui pouvaient m'instruire."
appraisal_events.explanation: Rather than take offense when the narrator's visible disappointment reveals that Elstir was once the ridiculed Verdurin-circle painter 'M. Biche,' Elstir responds with magnanimity, turning the awkward moment into instruction; the narrator explicitly frames this as the conduct of 'a true master.'

appraisal_events.evidence: "Il fut pris d'une joie dont il ne fut pas plus le maître... ma grand'mère fut beaucoup plus touchée de voir tous les efforts qu'il avait faits (sans y réussir) pour contenir la joie qui le secouait, que par tous les remerciements qu'il aurait pu proférer."
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup's uncontainable, childlike joy at receiving the Proudhon letters touches the grandmother more deeply than any words of thanks, casting him warmly as sincere and unguarded.

appraisal_events.evidence: "le directeur qui, consulté, répondit que, voiture ou petit chemin de fer, 'ce serait à peu près équivoque.' Il entendait signifier par là que ce serait équivalent (en somme, à peu près ce que Françoise eût exprimé en disant que 'cela reviendrait du pareil au même')"
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator gently mocks the hotel director's malapropism (using 'équivoque' for 'équivalent'), likening his pretension to elevated diction to the folk phrasing of the servant Françoise.

status_effects.explanation: Despite the discreditable revelation of his past as 'M. Biche' in the Verdurin circle, Elstir's generous, teacherly response to the narrator's evident disappointment locally elevates him as a wise, magnanimous 'true master.'
His spontaneous, barely-controlled joy at the grandmother's gift is presented as more moving than formal gratitude would have been, casting him favorably.
His fumbled use of an elevated word, likened to a servant's malapropism, mildly deflates his pretension to refined speech.

ambiguities: The passage raises but does not resolve a tension in Elstir's positioning: the revelation that he was once 'M. Biche,' 'le peintre ridicule et pervers, adopté jadis par les Verdurin,' causes the narrator real 'déception extraordinaire,' which could be read as a local discredit; however, since Elstir's own magnanimous conduct immediately follows and dominates the narrator's framing, the scene was scored as net elevation rather than diminishment.

The candidate 'le peintre' is not scored as a distinct character: within the passage it refers variously to Elstir himself (already captured under S1 and the accepted annotation's E1), to a generalized hypothetical 'grand peintre' in the essayistic theory of portraiture, and to an anonymous 'plus grand des peintres naturalistes' who painted the princesse de Luxembourg's unnamed cousin — none of these referents constitute an independently identifiable, scorable character.

princesse de Luxembourg is mentioned only as a genealogical anchor ('une cousine de la princesse de Luxembourg'); the unflattering portrait event targets her unnamed cousin, not the princesse herself, so she was not scored.
